headline: Cambridge puts ShotSpotter debate before 40 residents in first civic assembly
dek: A lottery-backed panel will study gunshot detection and park cameras over four Saturdays before sending recommendations to the City Council.
body: Cambridge is moving its argument over gunshot-detection technology and public surveillance into a new phase: a 40-person civic assembly selected through a resident lottery. The city scheduled the selection for Monday, Oct. 5, at City Hall, describing the process as the first municipal civic assembly in Massachusetts and one of the first in New England. The [City of Cambridge’s announcement](https://www.cambridgema.gov/news/2026/09/cityofcambridgetohostcivicassemblylotteryselectionnightonoctober5) said the panel will study the issues and develop recommendations for the City Council rather than make a binding decision itself.

The assembly’s assignment is deliberately narrow but consequential. Members will consider whether, how and under what conditions Cambridge should use gunshot-detection systems such as ShotSpotter and overnight video surveillance in public parks. The city’s [Civic Assembly guide](https://www.cambridgema.gov/civicassembly) says participants will examine effectiveness, cost, privacy, civil liberties, equity and public trust, then weigh evidence and lived experience before writing recommendations. Final authority remains with the elected council.

The selection process was designed to make the panel broader than the group that normally attends a council meeting. In September, the city mailed invitations to about 15,000 randomly selected households from a pool of roughly 56,000 Cambridge households. More than 400 people entered the lottery, according to the city, and every neighborhood was represented among the applicants. Residents 16 and older were eligible to volunteer, with additional outreach aimed at neighborhoods most affected by gun violence.

The city is also paying residents for the time required to do the work. The assembly will meet for four full Saturdays — Oct. 24, Nov. 7, Nov. 21 and Dec. 5 — with a $1,000 stipend and accommodations that include child care, interpretation and translation, according to the city’s September launch announcement. Independent experts and community members with different perspectives are expected to brief the panel. The process is being organized with FIDE North America and supported by community partners, including researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

The experiment follows a year of sharp disagreement over ShotSpotter. Cambridge Day reported that the City Council voted 5-2-2 in May to end the city’s use of the system within 90 days. The technology uses acoustic sensors to flag sounds that may be gunfire, a design supporters associate with faster emergency response and critics associate with privacy, accuracy and over-policing concerns. Those competing claims are part of what the assembly is being asked to examine; the city’s materials do not predetermine an outcome.

The debate changed again after the July 4 fatal shooting of Xavier Bautista, a Cambridge Department of Public Works employee. NBC Boston reported that the council later voted 6-3 to reactivate ShotSpotter for at least 90 days while the resident review took place. That sequence left Cambridge with a live policy question rather than a settled one: whether to keep a controversial detection network, impose new safeguards, or pursue other public-safety approaches.

For residents who were not selected, the process is still meant to be public. The city says briefings, agendas, speaker lists, minutes and other materials will be posted online, and community members can submit comments for the assembly and the city to consider. The city’s timeline says selected participants will be notified by Oct. 10, with recommendations due to the council in December. The council will then decide how — or whether — to incorporate them into future surveillance and public-safety policy.

That timetable gives Cambridge a structured way to test a difficult local question before making a longer-term commitment. It also creates a record residents can inspect: who was selected, what evidence the panel heard, which safeguards it recommends and where disagreement remains. The immediate result of the lottery is therefore only the beginning. The more consequential measure will be whether four Saturdays of representative deliberation produce guidance the council and the wider community consider credible.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Cambridge civic assembly takes up ShotSpotter debate
seoDescription: Cambridge is selecting 40 residents for a civic assembly that will study ShotSpotter and park surveillance before advising the City Council.
